verdict.rationale: Omarchy documents a generic USB ISO install, dual-booting beside Windows or other OSes, and running on modest hardware such as a 2011 ThinkPad X220. Community reports confirm installs on a desktop and a cheap Chromebook, though on the Chromebook the ISO route failed and the user had to fall back to archinstall. Graphics setup is promised only 'on supported hardware', and 'no vendor lock-in' is only implied by its Arch base (it uses Arch's package mirrors), so the story is delivered with real caveats. Missing for 10: a documented hardware compatibility list, explicit first-party statements on avoiding vendor lock-in, and reliable ISO install across diverse hardware.

support.subject: As a power-user, I can install and use the OS without vendor lock-in on hardware of my choosing

citations.quote: Write the ISO to a USB stick and answer five questions. It hands back a finished desktop.
you're able to install Omarchy to a single partition alongside Windows or other installations.
Even a 2011 ThinkPad X220 with 2GB of RAM can run Omarchy, with room to spare.
Graphics drivers and configuration, including NVIDIA on supported hardware, are sorted during installation.
Installed Omarchy on a €30 N23 Chromebook with a 32GB SSD. The ISO route failed and I fell back to archinstall
